newsitem.title: CHINA: China dissident says court refuses to accept suit.
newsitem.headline: China dissident says court refuses to accept suit.

text.p: Chinese dissident Bao Ge said on Wednesday that he planned to appeal against a court decision to reject his lawsuit against a labour camp for violating his human rights.
"The court told me that under Chinese law there is no provision for suing prisons or labour camps," he said in an interview with Reuters.

Bao, 33, was released on June 4 from the Shanghai Number One Labour Camp, where he served three years of "re-education through labour", an administrative punishment imposed by the police without a judicial trial.
This month, Bao applied to the Shanghai Xuhui District People's Court to sue the labour camp for what he said were a variety of human rights violations.
In a verdict reached on July 16 and issued to Bao on Wednesday, the court said it would not accept his lawsuit.
Bao had 10 days from the date of the decision to appeal to the Shanghai Number One Intermediate People's Court, a higher court, said the verdict, a copy of which was seen by Reuters.
In his original lawsuit, lodged with the court on July 11, Bao said the labour camp illegally confined him and restricted his right to write letters, receive visitors and vote.
He had not been permitted to appeal his sentence, or to read books he had taken to the prison camp, including his Bible, he said.
Relatives had been threatened and searched when they visited him and records of their conversations had been kept, he said.

Letters he wrote were screened, he was not allowed to receive books sent by relatives or to have pens and pencils, and he was not permitted to leave the prison to visit a dying relative, all of which violated regulations on re-education through labour, he said.

Bao had been a member of the Shanghai-based Association for Human Rights and was a campaigner for compensation from Tokyo for Chinese victims of Japanese war atrocities -- a sensitive issue after Beijing signed away all such claims in the 1970s.
He has been jailed frequently, and said on Wednesday that he had been followed by police since his release last month.

Last week, Bao wrote an open letter to China's parliament, the National People's Congress, calling on the government to honour the constitution in upholding the rights of workers and peasants and to end official corruption.
China's ruling Communist Party has identified corruption among officials as one of the greatest threats to its mandate and has initiated several campaigns to stamp it out.
